Question #1

17/5 gives full decimal answer (3.4), while 17 %/% 5 gives the whole number quotient (3) and 17 %% 5 gives the leftover remainder(2) which together reconstruct the original number (3x5) + 2 = 17.

##Part B
```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i

typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)

class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)

mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```
Question #3
In R the numbers are stored by default as double precision floating points like ("double").Assigning x <- 42 makes a numeric double and the L (y <- 42L) tells R to store it as a true integer in memory.

Question #4 
Yes because typeof(),class(), and mode() can differ depending on object structure. like both x and y return mode() as numeric but their typeof() returns double and integer for complex data structures like a matrix, typeof() returns double or whatever underlying atomic data type it contains.

##Part C
```{r}
num_string <- "123"
num_val <- as.numeric(num_string)
typeof(num_val)
class(num_val)
mode(num_val)

as.logical(0)
as.logical(1)

bad_string <- "hello123"
as.numeric(bad_string)
```
Question #5
Why a warning instead of crashing:
I think its to keep a large scripts running smoothly even if a few data values fail to convert, replacing bad values with NA so the whole process doesn't stop.

Risks of ignoring warnings:
Unexpected NA values can quietly pass into later calculations, causing wrong results without you noticing.

Question #6
as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1) produce both return TRUE.
The Rule R follows 0 is FALSE and any non-zero number is TRUE.

##Part D
```{r}
first_name <- "juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"

print(first_name)
print(last_name)
cat(first_name, last_name)
```
```{r}
paste(first_name, last_name)
paste0(first_name, last_name)
```
```{r}
paste(first_name, last_name, sep = "-")
```
```{r}
age <- 21 
full_name <- paste(first_name, last_name)
paste0(full_name, " is ",  age, " years old.")
```
Question #7 
paste() adds a space between strings by default ( sep = " "), while paste0() joins them directly with zero seprator space ( sep = "").

Question #8
No error occured because paste0() automatically converts non-characters types like age into strings (type coercion) before joining them.

##Part E
```{r}
"5" + 5
```
```{r}
as.numeric("5") + 5
```
Question #9
Because R strictly seperates math operations from string operations
to prevent unintended logical errors in data analysis. Requiring explicit conversion with as.numeric() ensures programmers intentionally choose when to convert text to numbers rather than relying on automatic guessing.

Question #10
The column was imported as character strings rather than numbers. To diagnose, run typeof(), class(), or mode() on the column. To fix it, convert the entire column using as.numeric text into numbers so sum() works properly.

Conclusion: 
In R, data types like double,integer,character, and logical govern how functions process variables. using functions such as typeof()
and class() helps inspect object structures and prevent unexpected runtime errors before performing mathematical or logical calculations. Explicitly converting data types with functions like as.numeric() ensures calculations run accurately without silent coercion issues.



## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.
